content: If you have diabetes, this medication may influence your blood sugar levels. It is essential to monitor your blood sugar regularly as instructed and share the results with your doctor. Notify your doctor immediately if you experience symptoms of high blood sugar, such as increased thirst or urination. Inform your doctor if you have recently undergone surgery, are planning to have surgery, or if you will be confined to a bed or chair for an extended period (e.g., during a long plane flight). These conditions can elevate your risk of developing blood clots, particularly if you are using hormonal birth control. This medication may cause blotchy, dark areas on your face and skin, a condition known as melasma. Sunlight can exacerbate this effect, so it is advisable to limit your time in the sun and avoid tanning booths and sunlamps. If you are nearsighted or wear contact lenses, you may experience vision problems or difficulty wearing your lenses while on this medication. Additionally, it may take longer for you to conceive after discontinuing birth control pills. This medication should not be used during pregnancy. If you become pregnant or suspect you might be pregnant, inform your doctor immediately. It may also reduce breast milk production, and a small amount of the medication can pass into breast milk, potentially causing undesirable effects in a nursing infant. Drug interactions can alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Some drugs may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal birth control by decreasing the levels of birth control hormones in your body, which can result in pregnancy. Examples include griseofulvin, modafinil, rifamycins (such as rifampin, rifabutin), ritonavir, and St. John’s Wort. Inform your doctor when starting any new medication and discuss whether you should use reliable backup birth control. This medication may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as blood tests for clotting factors or thyroid function, potentially leading to false test results. In the event of an overdose, if someone exhibits severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. While taking this medication, regular complete physical exams, including lab and/or medical tests (e.g., blood pressure, breast exam, pelvic exam, Pap smear), should be conducted. Follow your doctor’s instructions for self-examining your breasts and report any lumps immediately. Keep all medical and lab appointments. If you miss a dose, the advice on what to do depends on the brand of medication and the number of doses missed. Refer to the product package information for specific instructions. You may need to use backup birth control methods, such as condoms or spermicides, to prevent pregnancy. Store this medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not contain all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs. Do not use this medication if you smoke cigarettes or use tobacco and are over 35 years old. Smoking increases your risk of stroke, heart attack, blood clots, and high blood pressure when using hormonal birth control (such as the pill, patch, or ring). The risk of these serious problems increases with age and the number of cigarettes smoked. This combination hormone medication is used to prevent pregnancy. Read the Patient Information Leaflet provided by your pharmacist before starting this medication and each time you get a refill. The leaflet contains critical information on when to take your pills and what to do if you miss a dose. Take this medication by mouth as directed by your doctor, usually once daily. It is crucial to take this medication exactly as prescribed. With certain brands of birth control pills, the amount of estrogen and progestin in each active tablet varies at different times in the cycle. Follow the package instructions to find the first tablet, start with the first tablet in the pack, and take them in the correct order. Do not skip any doses. If you experience vomiting or diarrhea within 3 to 4 hours after taking your tablet, refer to the Patient Information Leaflet section titled What to Do if You Miss Tablets. Taking this medication after your evening meal or at bedtime may help if you experience stomach upset or nausea. You may choose to take it at another time of day that is easier for you to remember. Your pill pack contains 26 pills with active medication and 2 reminder pills with no medication. Take one active pill (with hormones) once daily for 26 consecutive days. After taking the last active pill, take one reminder pill daily for 2 consecutive days unless otherwise directed by your doctor. You should have your period during the fourth week of the cycle. After taking the last reminder tablet in the pack, start a new pack the next day, even if your period is still ongoing or if you do not have your period. If this is your first time using this medication and you are not switching from another form of hormonal birth control (such as a patch or other birth control pills), take the first tablet in the pack on the first day of your period. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for information on how to switch from other forms of hormonal birth control to this product. Common side effects may include nausea, vomiting, headache, abdominal cramps or bloating, breast tenderness, swelling of the ankles or feet (fluid retention), or weight changes. Vaginal bleeding between periods (spotting) or missed/irregular periods may occur, especially during the first few months of use. If any of these effects persist or worsen, inform your doctor or pharmacist promptly. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefit to you outweighs the risk of side effects. This medication may increase your blood pressure. Rarely, it may cause serious (sometimes fatal) problems from blood clots, such as heart attack, stroke, or blood clots in the lungs or legs. A very serious allergic reaction to this drug is rare. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. Before using this medication, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to estradiol or dienogest, or to any estrogens (such as mestranol) or progestins (such as norethindrone, desogestrel), or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other problems.
